title.text:
AI and machine learning:
the map before the route

objects.text: What do I need to understand about AI before I decide anything about it?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 0, the introduction
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome. Before we build anything, we spend one session on the ideas that sit under all of it: how AI and machine learning actually work, what the jobs and fields are, and why a company leader needs this picture. There are no exercises today. You will leave with a handbook to read before Session 1.

The question for today is this: What do I need to understand about AI before I decide anything about it? Keep it in mind. At the end of the session we come back to it and see how much more you can say.

title.text: Your two hours: ideas and questions, no activities

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_d1a6bf28.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: There are no exercises today. Stop me at any point with a question.

slides.notes:
Today is for understanding, so there are no exercises. The first half covers how AI and machine learning work and how a model is measured. After the break come data readiness, what happens behind a chat message, foundation models and costs, and then industry, roles and the road ahead.

It is a full session, so keep a note of any question we have to park. Ask your question when it comes to you. It will help everyone.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: The thing that has learned patterns and makes the predictions.
One of the many settings inside a model that training adjusts. Also called a weight.
Showing the model many examples and adjusting its settings until its errors shrink.
Using a trained model to make a prediction or write an answer.
When a model memorises its examples and fails on new ones.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_robot_0.70.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_switch_0.70.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_book_0.70.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_speech_0.70.png

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Model. The thing that has learned patterns and makes the predictions.

Parameter. One of the many settings inside a model that training adjusts. Also called a weight.

Training. Showing the model many examples and adjusting its settings until its errors shrink.

Inference. Using a trained model to make a prediction or write an answer.

Overfitting. When a model memorises its examples and fails on new ones.

title.text:
Today gives you the words and the
picture that every later session uses

objects.text: You can ask your team sharp questions when you know who does what.

slides.notes:
Let me start with why this session matters. Executives who skip the basics tend to be swayed by confident vendors and by confident-sounding tools. Four things change once you have the picture. You can judge a vendor’s claim, because you know how the thing learns. You can choose a good first task, because you know what AI is good at.

You can check a result, because you know why models fail. And you can question your team well, because you know who does what. Which of those would help you most this month?

title.text:
Today’s ideas come back in
every phase of the course

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_abeb9445.png
objects.alt: Today’s ideas come back in every phase of the course

objects.text: Session 0 is the map. The next twelve sessions are the route.

slides.notes:
Here is the whole course in four steps. First you choose one real task from your company and learn how AI fails on it. Then you prepare your information and review documents. Then I show you two small automations, one by rules and one with AI, and what they save.

Finally you write the rules, question vendors, build the business case and plan the next ninety days. Every one of those steps uses an idea from today: how a model learns, what data it needs, and where it breaks. Today is the map. The rest is the route.

title.text: AI is a family: each layer sits inside the one above

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_stack_7.70x4.80_a867d088.png
objects.alt: AI is a family: each layer sits inside the one above

objects.text: Most tools in the news today are generative AI, the innermost layer.

runs.text: Rules came first: a person writes every step.
Machine learning finds the steps from examples.

slides.notes:
Start with the family tree. Artificial intelligence is the broad idea: software doing tasks we link with human thinking. Early AI was rules written by people. Machine learning is a smarter branch: instead of writing every rule, we show the computer examples and it finds the pattern. Deep learning is machine learning using large neural networks, and it is behind most progress in images, speech and language.

Generative AI sits inside that: models that create new text, pictures or code. When someone says AI today, they usually mean that inner circle.

title.text:
AI has several fields; each one
suits a different business problem

rows.text: Read invoices, check goods in photos
Turns speech into text and back
Suggests what a person may want next
Creates new text, images or code

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_phone_0.34.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_chart_0.34.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_tag_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_flag_0.34.png

slides.notes:
Here are the main fields. Natural language processing is working with human language: summarising, sorting and translating. Computer vision reads images, such as invoices or photos of damaged goods. Speech turns calls and meetings into text. Forecasting predicts numbers over time. Recommendation suggests what to offer next. Anomaly detection spots what does not fit, which is how many fraud alerts work.

And generative AI creates drafts. Which of these have you already met in your company, perhaps without calling it AI?

title.text: Machines learn in four main ways

rows.text: From examples with the right answer attached
Flag fraud, rate credit risk, predict a price
Finds groups and patterns, with no answers given
By predicting a hidden part of its own data
Language models predicting the next word

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_gear_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_speech_0.50.png

objects.text: Supervised work has two kinds: classification picks a category, such as will this invoice be paid late, yes or no; regression predicts a number, such as next month’s sales.

slides.notes:
Four ways machines learn. Supervised learning uses examples with the right answer attached, like past invoices marked paid on time or late. It comes in two kinds. Classification chooses a category. Regression predicts a number. Unsupervised learning is given no answers and finds groups, like customer segments. Reinforcement learning learns by trial and reward, useful for routing and pricing.

Self-supervised learning hides part of its own data and learns to predict it, and that is how language models learn the next word. Most business AI you will meet is supervised or self-supervised.

title.text:
Training is a loop: guess,
measure the error, adjust, repeat

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_cycle_7.70x4.80_54281ed0.png
objects.alt: Training is a loop: guess, measure the error, adjust, repeat

objects.text: A model starts with random settings and improves by repetition.

runs.text: The settings are called parameters or weights.
The error is measured with a number called loss.
Large models repeat this loop millions of times.

slides.notes:
Here is the core idea of how machines learn. A model starts with random settings, called parameters or weights. It makes a guess, we measure how wrong it was with a number called the loss, and then the settings are adjusted a little so that the next guess is less wrong.

Then it repeats, again and again, over many examples. Nothing mysterious: guess, measure the error, adjust, repeat. A large model repeats this loop millions of times. The next two slides explain how it knows which way to adjust.

title.text:
Gradient descent finds lower error
by taking small steps downhill

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_descent_7.70x4.80_da71a2dc.png
objects.alt: Gradient descent finds lower error by taking small steps downhill

objects.text: Think of walking down a hill in fog: you feel the slope and step downhill.

runs.text: The slope tells the model which way reduces the error.
The learning rate is the step size: too big overshoots, too small is slow.
It usually finds a good low point, and sometimes only a local one.

slides.notes:
Gradient descent is the method that decides which way to adjust. Picture walking down a hill in thick fog. You cannot see the valley, but you can feel the slope under your feet, so you step downhill. In a model, the error is the height, and the settings are your position.

The slope tells the model which way lowers the error. The step size is called the learning rate. Too big and you overshoot, too small and you take forever. It reaches a good low point, though not always the lowest possible one.

title.text:
Backpropagation shares the blame
for an error back through the network

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_network_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Backpropagation shares the blame for an error back through the network

objects.text: The network guesses forward. The error then travels backward and each connection learns how much it caused.

runs.text: Each connection is nudged to cause less error next time.
Gradient descent uses these blame figures to take its step.
Together they train almost every modern neural network.

slides.notes:
Now a neural network. It is layers of simple units joined by connections, each with a weight. Information flows forward and produces a guess. Backpropagation then sends the error backward, layer by layer, working out how much each connection contributed to the mistake. That share of the blame is what gradient descent uses to adjust each weight.

You do not need the mathematics. Remember the shape: guess forward, blame backward, adjust, repeat. It is how nearly every modern neural network, including language models, is trained.

title.text: Keep three sets of data apart: train, check and test

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_d9ec1232.png
objects.alt: Keep three sets of data apart: train, check and test

objects.text: The test set stays locked until you have chosen your model.

slides.notes:
To know whether a model really works, we split the data into three. Training data is what the model learns from. Validation data is used while you build, to compare versions and tune settings. Test data stays locked away until the end and is used once for an honest score.

If you keep checking the test set while you build, you start fitting the model to the test, and the score stops being honest. When a vendor quotes an accuracy figure, ask which of these three it was measured on.

title.text:
A model can memorise: always
judge it on data it has never seen

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_versus_7.70x4.80_79b5c9dc.png
objects.alt: A model can memorise: always judge it on data it has never seen

objects.text: Overfitting is when a model learns its examples by heart.

runs.text: It looks excellent on old data and fails on new cases.
More varied data and a simpler model help.
A locked test set is the check.

slides.notes:
This is overfitting, the most common way models disappoint. A student who memorises last year’s answers does perfectly on those questions and badly on new ones. A model can do the same. The numbers on this slide are illustrative, but the pattern is real: very high accuracy on the data it trained on, much lower on new data.

The remedy is more varied data, a simpler model, and always judging on data the model has never seen. That is why a vendor’s demo on their own data tells you little.

title.text:
Accuracy alone can mislead:
count the four kinds of answer

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_confusion_7.70x4.80_b212e4df.png
objects.alt: Accuracy alone can mislead: count the four kinds of answer

objects.text: A fraud model checks 1,000 payments. Ten are really fraud. These numbers are illustrative.

runs.text: Accuracy is 986 right out of 1,000, or 98.6%.
A model that says fine every time scores 99% and catches nothing.

slides.notes:
Accuracy sounds simple: how often is the model right. It can mislead badly. Imagine a fraud model that checks a thousand payments, of which ten are really fraud. It catches eight, raises twelve false alarms, misses two, and correctly clears nine hundred and seventy-eight. That is accuracy of ninety-eight point six percent, which sounds superb.

But a model that said fine every single time would score ninety-nine percent and catch nothing. The four boxes are called the confusion matrix. Each kind of mistake has a different cost to your business. The numbers are illustrative. Which mistake would hurt you more, a false alarm or a miss?

title.text: Precision, recall and F1 answer different questions

rows.text: How often is it right overall?
When it says fraud, how often is it right?
Of the real fraud, how much did it catch?
One number that balances precision and recall

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.39.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_flag_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.50.png

objects.text: Raise the threshold and precision usually rises while recall falls. Choose by what a miss and a false alarm cost you.

slides.notes:
From those four boxes come three measures. Precision asks: when the model says fraud, how often is it right?

Here eight of twenty, so forty percent. Recall asks: of the real fraud, how much did it catch?

Eight of ten, so eighty percent. F1 blends the two into one number, about fifty-three percent. Accuracy, precision and recall answer different questions, and you cannot read one without the others. Raise the threshold and precision usually rises while recall falls. So the right balance depends on what a miss and a false alarm cost you. When a vendor quotes one figure, ask for the other two.

title.text:
ROC and AUC show how good
a model is at every threshold

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_roc_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: ROC and AUC show how good a model is at every threshold

objects.text: Each point on the curve is one threshold: how much fraud you catch against how many false alarms you raise.

runs.text: AUC is the area under the curve. 1.0 is perfect and 0.5 is a coin flip.
This picture shows about 0.86 (illustrative).
For rare events, also check precision.

slides.notes:
Models usually give a score, and you choose a threshold above which you act. The ROC curve shows what happens at every threshold. Each point is one setting: how much of the real fraud you catch, against how many false alarms you raise. The dashed line is a coin flip.

The area under the curve is called AUC. One point zero is perfect, and zero point five is no better than chance. In this picture it is about zero point eight six, which is illustrative. AUC is useful for comparing models. For rare events, also look at precision, because AUC can look good while most alerts are false alarms.

title.text: Pick the measure that fits the task

rows.text: Yes or no, or a category
What does a miss cost, and a false alarm?
How far off is a typical forecast, in our units?
Is the right item in the first few suggestions?
Is the answer supported by our documents?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_flag_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_tag_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_speech_0.50.png

objects.text: MAE is the average miss. RMSE punishes big misses more. For any quoted figure ask: measured on which data, at which threshold?

slides.notes:
Different tasks need different measures. For yes or no and category tasks, use precision, recall, F1 and AUC. For predicting numbers, use the average miss, called MAE, and RMSE, which punishes big misses more. For ranking and suggestions, ask whether the right item appears in the first few results.

For language models there is no single score. We look at whether the answer is supported by your documents, whether the citations are right, and what a person reviewing the answers says. The habit that matters: for any figure quoted to you, ask which data it was measured on, and at what threshold. Then ask what a miss costs.

title.text:
Benchmarks compare models,
but they do not test your task

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.75.png

objects.text: What they give you

runs.text: Standard questions every model answers
Scores for knowledge, coding and maths
Public rankings built from human votes

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_cross_0.75.png

objects.text: Their limits

runs.text: Test answers can leak into training data
Many scores are published by the vendor
Your documents and risks are not in them

objects.text: Use them to shortlist, then test on 50 of your own questions.

slides.notes:
Vendors often quote benchmarks. A benchmark is a standard set of test questions that every model answers, so scores can be compared. MMLU tests broad knowledge, HumanEval tests writing code, and Chatbot Arena ranks models by human votes. They are useful for a shortlist. But they have limits.

Test answers can leak into the training data, many scores are published by the vendor itself, and none of them contain your documents, your language or your risks. So use benchmarks to shortlist, then test the finalists on fifty of your own questions with known answers. We practise that in Session 10.

title.text:
Companies hold five kinds of data,
and most of it is unstructured

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_icons_7.70x4.80_955a4580.png
objects.alt: Companies hold five kinds of data, and most of it is unstructured

objects.text: Tables are structured. Text, images and sound are unstructured.

runs.text: Labelled data has the right answer attached.
Unlabelled data does not.
Time series is data in order of time, such as daily sales.

slides.notes:
Now data, the raw material. Companies hold tables such as invoices and sales sheets; text such as emails and contracts; images such as photos of goods and scanned documents; sound such as calls and meetings; and sensor readings such as machine data or vehicle tracking. Tables are called structured data.

The rest is unstructured, and it is most of what a company holds. Data may also be labelled, with the right answer attached, or unlabelled. And time series means values in order of time, like daily sales. Which kind does your task use?

title.text: Data quality decides what a model can learn

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_folder_0.70.png

objects.text: Complete: no large gaps.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.70.png

objects.text: Correct: figures match the source.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_calendar_0.70.png

objects.text: Current: not out of date.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_tag_0.70.png

objects.text: Consistent: one name and one format for one thing.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_people_0.70.png

objects.text: Representative: it covers the cases you will meet.

slides.notes:
A model can only learn from what it is shown. Five questions about data quality. Is it complete, with no large gaps?

Is it correct, matching the source?

Is it current, or out of date?

Is it consistent, using one name and one format for one thing?

And is it representative, covering the cases the model will meet?

If the data under-represents a group of customers, the model will be worse for them. That is how bias enters. And remember that personal data is covered by the Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019, so check your duties with a lawyer.

title.text:
Is your data ready for AI? A law
firm shows the questions to ask

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_icons_7.70x4.80_75d037f4.png
objects.alt: Is your data ready for AI? A law firm shows the questions to ask

objects.text: Thirty years of decisions and rulings sit in five places and five formats.

runs.text: A scan is only a picture until text is read from it.
AI can use only what is readable, findable and allowed.

slides.notes:
Now a question every organisation faces: is our data ready for AI?

Take a law firm with thirty years of decisions and rulings. Some are paper files in a records room. Some are scanned PDFs on a shared drive, of mixed quality. Some are Word drafts, some sit inside emails, and a spreadsheet index lists part of it, partly out of date.

A model cannot use paper. A scan is only a picture until text is read from it. And nothing should be used until you know who owns it and whether it is confidential. So readiness has three tests: is it readable, is it findable, and is it allowed?

title.text:
Score each area before you
spend: the readiness scorecard

rows.text: Do we know what exists and where?
Can a machine read the text?
Who may use it, and for what?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_folder_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.39.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_doc_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_tag_0.39.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_lock_0.39.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_calendar_0.50.png

slides.notes:
Before spending, score the data on six areas. Inventory: do we know what exists and where?

Readable: can a machine read the text, or are scans crooked and faint?

Complete and unique: are there gaps, and ten copies of the same ruling?

Metadata: do we know the court, date, parties and citation, or only a file name?

Rights: who may use it and for what, including client privilege and personal data?

And current: are overruled decisions mixed in with good law?

Score each green, amber or red. A red on rights stops the project until a lawyer has looked at it. Where does your biggest red sit?

title.text: Six steps turn a records room into AI-ready data

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_105ae73c.png
objects.alt: Six steps turn a records room into AI-ready data

objects.text: Start with one court and ten years. Test it, then widen.

slides.notes:
Six steps take the law firm from a records room to AI-ready data. One, inventory: list every source, its owner and its format. Two, digitise: scan the paper and run OCR to read the text. Three, clean: remove duplicates and fix obvious errors. Four, describe: add court, date, parties and citation as labels.

Five, protect: set who can see what, and mask personal data where needed. Six, index and test: chunk, embed and index, then ask fifty real questions with known answers and measure what comes back. Start small, with one court and ten years. Skipping the testing step is the usual mistake.

title.text:
Preparing data to search it is lighter
than preparing it to train a model

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.75.png

objects.text: For retrieval

runs.text: Readable text with labels
Cut into chunks and indexed
Updated when documents change
Answers can cite the source

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_gear_0.75.png

objects.text: For training or fine-tuning

runs.text: Right to use the data confirmed
Personal data removed
Formatted as examples, such as questions and answers
Split into train, validation and test sets

objects.text: Most organisations should prepare for retrieval first.

slides.notes:
Preparing data depends on what you want to do with it. To search it, which is retrieval, you need readable text with labels, cut into chunks and indexed, kept up to date, so answers can point to the source. To train or fine-tune a model, you need more.

You need a confirmed right to use the data, personal data removed, quality filtered, the content formatted as examples such as question and answer pairs, and split into training, validation and test sets. That is a bigger project. So most organisations should prepare for retrieval first, and consider fine-tuning only when prompting and retrieval have clearly reached a limit. Check your duties with a lawyer.

title.text: A language model is trained in stages

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_97d2f19f.png
objects.alt: A language model is trained in stages

objects.text: It writes likely text. It does not look facts up unless search or files are switched on.

slides.notes:
How does a language model like the assistants you use come about?

It reads a huge amount of text. It practises guessing the next word, again and again, which is the self-supervised learning we saw. Then it is tuned to follow instructions, and people rate its answers so that it improves. When you use it, it predicts the next word, then the next.

That explains the strengths and the weakness. It writes fluent, likely text. It does not look facts up unless search or files are switched on, which is why it can sound sure and be wrong.

title.text:
Training builds the model once;
inference uses it every time

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_versus_7.70x4.80_c3b55826.png
objects.alt: Training builds the model once; inference uses it every time

objects.text: Most companies only ever do inference.

runs.text: Training needs large data and heavy computing.
Inference needs speed, and its cost grows with use.

slides.notes:
Two words that explain a lot of the cost and the risk. Training is the learning phase we described earlier. It is rare, needs large data and heavy computing, and produces a model file. Inference is using that model, every time someone sends a request. It must be fast, and its cost grows with the number of requests.

Most companies never train anything. They pay for inference, or run an existing model themselves. When a vendor says it trained on your data, ask whether they mean training, or only that your files are searched at inference time. Those are very different.

title.text:
Behind the screen: what happens
when you send a message with a file

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_e721491b.png
objects.alt: Behind the screen: what happens when you send a message with a file

objects.text: With no file, only the last step happens: your words become tokens and the model predicts the reply.

slides.notes:
Now let us look behind the screen. You type a question and attach a contract. First the system reads the file and pulls out the text. A scan needs optical character recognition first. The text is cut into passages called chunks. Each chunk is turned into an embedding, a list of numbers that captures its meaning.

The embeddings are stored in an index, often called a vector database. Your question is also turned into an embedding, and the closest chunks are retrieved. The question, those chunks and the rules are assembled into one prompt. The model then writes the answer one token at a time, and may cite the chunks.

With a short file, many products simply place the whole file in the prompt. Details differ by vendor.

title.text:
Each stage can fail, and the
failure shows in the answer

rows.text: Gets text out of the file
A scan is misread; tables scramble
A clause is split across two chunks
The index is out of date
The wrong passage returns; access rights are ignored
It adds claims the passages do not support

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_doc_0.39.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_grid_0.39.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_folder_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_robot_0.50.png

slides.notes:
Each stage can fail, and the failure shows up in the answer. If the scan is misread at the first stage, everything after is built on errors. If a clause is cut across two chunks, the model may see half of it. If the index is old, you get yesterday’s answer.

If retrieval returns the wrong passage, the model answers confidently from it. If the system ignores who may see which file, a person can read what they should not. And at the last stage the model can add claims the passages do not support. So when an answer is wrong, ask which stage failed.

This is why we test on your own documents in Session 5.

title.text:
Most companies use a foundation
model that someone else trained

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_stack_7.70x4.80_54e49645.png
objects.alt: Most companies use a foundation model that someone else trained

objects.text: A foundation model is a large model trained once, then adapted to many tasks.

runs.text: Training one takes huge data and computing power, so few organisations do it.
You choose which one to rent or download.

slides.notes:
Most companies do not train their own large model. A foundation model is a very large model trained once on broad data, then adapted to many tasks. Training one takes a very large amount of data and computing power, so only a few organisations do it. What you choose is which one to rent or download, and how to adapt it.

Think of four layers. The foundation model sits at the bottom. Your adaptation sits above it: prompts, retrieval or fine-tuning. Your product sits on top: a tool, a workflow or an agent. And under all of it are your data and your people, which no vendor supplies.

title.text:
Proprietary or open-weight: you
choose control or convenience

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_cloud_0.75.png

objects.text: Proprietary, rented

runs.text: Reached by subscription or API
Little set-up; the vendor maintains it
Your data goes to the vendor

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_gear_0.75.png

objects.text: Open-weight, downloaded

runs.text: Runs on your own servers
You control where data goes
Needs skills and hardware
The licence may still limit use

objects.text: Open does not mean free or simple: you still pay to run and care for it.

slides.notes:
A common choice is proprietary or open. A proprietary model is reached by subscription or through an API. Set-up is easy and the vendor maintains it, but your data goes to the vendor under its terms. An open-weight model can be downloaded and run on your own servers, so you control where data goes.

You then need the skills and hardware to run it. The word open can mislead. Many open models carry licences that limit some uses, so read the licence. Open does not mean free or simple, because you still pay for running and care. For most companies starting out, a proprietary tool with clear data terms is usually the quicker path.

title.text: Four ways to adapt a model, from cheap to costly

rows.text: The facts the model can see
Answers must come from your documents
You need a steady format or tone at volume

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_speech_0.39.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_gear_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_book_0.50.png

objects.text: Fine-tuning teaches style and skill. Retrieval supplies facts. Most business needs start with prompting and retrieval.

slides.notes:
Four ways to adapt a model, from cheap to costly. Prompting changes the instructions you give. Always start there. Retrieval changes the facts the model can see, so answers come from your documents. Fine-tuning changes the model itself a little, teaching it a style or a skill, such as a steady format.

It does not reliably teach it new facts. Training from scratch changes everything and is almost never right for a company. So the rule: fine-tuning teaches style and skill, retrieval supplies facts. Most business needs are met by prompting and retrieval.

title.text: AI has five costs beyond the licence

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_coin_0.70.png

objects.text: Usage: tokens in and out, or seats.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_folder_0.70.png

objects.text: Data preparation: digitising, cleaning, describing.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_gear_0.70.png

objects.text: Set-up and integration with your systems.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_people_0.70.png

objects.text: People: review time, training and owners.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_bell_0.70.png

objects.text: Monitoring, upkeep and switching later.

slides.notes:
Finally, cost. The subscription is only the first line. Usage: language models are priced by tokens, a token being a piece of a word, for what goes in and what comes out, or by the seat. Data preparation: digitising, cleaning and describing your documents takes more effort than most people expect.

Set-up and integration: connecting the tool to your systems. People: review time, training and owners. And monitoring and upkeep, plus the cost of switching vendors later. I give no prices here, because they change often. Session 11 builds your costed case.

title.text: What AI does well and what it does badly

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.75.png

objects.text: Does well

runs.text: Finding patterns in large amounts of data
Drafting and summarising text
Working fast, without tiring
Sorting and flagging for a person to check

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_cross_0.75.png

objects.text: Does badly

runs.text: Knowing which fact is true
Rare events it has seen little of
Judging fairness or consequences
Staying correct when the world changes

objects.text: Use it where a quick check can catch a mistake.

slides.notes:
A balanced picture. AI does well at finding patterns in large amounts of data, drafting and summarising, working fast without tiring, and sorting or flagging things for a person to check. It does badly at knowing which fact is true, at rare events it has seen little of, at judging fairness or consequences, and at staying correct when the world changes.

The practical rule for the whole course: use AI where a quick check can catch a mistake. Keep people on decisions that carry risk. We turn that rule into a method in Session 1.

title.text: Where AI is used across industries

rows.text: Crop disease from photos, price forecasts

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_coin_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_plant_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_bag_0.38.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_clinic_0.38.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_people_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_phone_0.38.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.38.png

slides.notes:
Here is how those fields show up across industries. In banking and mobile money: fraud alerts and credit risk. In agriculture: reading crop disease from photos and forecasting prices. In retail and distribution: demand and route planning. In health administration: notes, scheduling and triage support. In HR: CV screening, which carries a bias risk.

In customer service: assistants and enquiry sorting. In finance: invoice reading and matching. Notice that the same few fields keep appearing. Which row is closest to your business, and which is furthest?

title.text: Who does what: the roles behind AI work

rows.text: Builds the pipes that bring clean data in
Explains what happened, with tables and charts
Builds and tests models that predict
Makes a model a reliable product
Invents new methods, mostly in labs
Chooses uses, sets rules, checks value

slides.notes:
Now the people. A data engineer builds the pipes that bring clean data in. A data analyst explains what happened, with tables and charts. A data scientist builds and tests models that predict or classify. A machine learning engineer turns a model into a reliable product. An MLOps engineer builds the systems that train, release and monitor models safely.

An applied AI engineer builds with ready-made models, which is closest to this course. An AI researcher invents new methods, mostly in labs. And the product or governance lead chooses the use cases and sets the rules. That seat is yours. A data steward, noted below, owns the quality and rights of the data. In a small company one person does several of these jobs.

title.text: The roles hand work to each other in a line

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_fe855007.png
objects.alt: The roles hand work to each other in a line

objects.text: At every step, a leader owns the question, the rules and the decision.

slides.notes:
Here is how the roles hand work along. The data engineer collects and cleans the data. The analyst finds patterns and measures. The scientist trains and tests a model. The machine learning engineer deploys and monitors it. And at every step, a leader owns the question, the rules and the decision.

That is the seat you occupy, whatever your title. If your company has none of these people, you can still do this work with ready-made tools, and that is exactly what the build sessions show. Where in this line would you want a specialist in your company?

title.text:
A model is never finished: it is trained,
tested, deployed and watched

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_cycle_7.70x4.80_e6db6cd9.png
objects.alt: A model is never finished: it is trained, tested, deployed and watched

objects.text: The world changes, so a model’s accuracy drifts.

runs.text: Drift: today’s data no longer looks like the training data.
Someone must own the monitoring and the off switch.
Every AI project needs an owner after the purchase.

slides.notes:
A model is not finished when it is trained. It is collected, trained, tested, deployed, and then watched. Customers change, prices change, fraud tactics change, and the data today stops looking like the data the model learned from. That is called drift, and accuracy slowly falls. So someone must own the monitoring and the off switch.

This is why every AI project needs an owner after the purchase, and it is why Sessions 7, 9 and 11 spend time on limits, risk and ownership.

title.text:
Rules, workflows and agents: the
more freedom, the more limits

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_ladder_7.70x4.80_970b1acc.png
objects.alt: Rules, workflows and agents: the more freedom, the more limits

objects.text: Each step up gains flexibility and loses predictability.

runs.text: Sessions 6 and 8 show the first two.
Session 7 sets the limits for the third.
Every step up needs stricter limits and a person to approve.

slides.notes:
One last picture before the roadmap. Automation comes in three levels of freedom. A rule-based robot follows fixed steps. A workflow follows a fixed path and has one AI step inside it. An agent is given a goal and chooses its own tools and steps. Each step up gains flexibility and loses predictability, so it needs stricter limits and a person to approve.

In the course I show you the first two, in Sessions 6 and 8, and in Session 7 you set the limits for the third. That is the whole arc in one slide.

rows.text: 1  Where AI fits in your business

Here are all twelve sessions and what you keep from each. You have seen the arc already. One task from your company runs through every row. In Session 1 you choose and measure it. In 2 and 3 you test it and brief a tool. In 4 and 5 you prepare its information and review documents.

In 6 and 8 I show you two automations. In 7 you set the limits. In 9 you write the risks and the policy, in 10 the vendor questions, in 11 the business case, and in 12 you show it and plan ninety days.

What you take home, and
what to prepare for Session 1

title.text:
Take the handbook home,
and choose your three tasks

objects.text: What you keep from today

runs.text: The Course Handbook, with today’s ideas, a glossary and what to prepare. Read it before Session 1.

objects.text: Our question today
What do I need to understand about AI before I decide anything about it?
Next session
Session 1: Where AI fits in your business. Bring three candidate tasks from your own company.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_card_4.10x4.50_d4e1fd2d.png

slides.notes:
Take the handbook home. It repeats today’s ideas with pictures and has a glossary you can search. Before Session 1, choose three recurring tasks from your company, and bring a laptop and one AI assistant account. If anything today was unclear, write the question down. We start Session 1 by answering it.

We began with this question: What do I need to understand about AI before I decide anything about it? Before you go, say in one sentence what you can now say about it.
